content: Tarnish is a layer of corrosion that forms on metals such as copper, brass, silver, and aluminum, as well as other semi-reactive metals, as a result of oxidation. This process is similar to rusting but occurs at a slower rate. Tarnish is primarily caused by chemical reactions with substances in the air, such as sulfur. It typically manifests as a gray or black film on the surface of the metal. To prevent tarnishing in objects that are primarily for display rather than regular use, a process called tinning can be employed. Tinning involves coating the reactive metal with a non-reactive substance, such as tin or wax, to create a protective barrier that prevents exposure to oxygen. For items that are used more frequently, such as silverware, tarnish can be effectively prevented through regular use and cleaning with mild dish soap. To remove tarnish, a safe and straightforward method involves a process akin to kitchen electrostripping. This technique is particularly effective for cleaning tarnish from flatware and hollowware. Begin by lining a pot with aluminum foil and preparing a diluted solution consisting of equal parts baking soda, salt, and liquid soap. A typical ratio is one-quarter cup of each ingredient per gallon of water. Place the tarnished silver in the pot, bring the solution to a simmer, and allow it to sit for 10–20 minutes. During this time, the oxides will transfer from the silver to the aluminum, which will darken as a result. Discard the aluminum foil and thoroughly wash the silver before use. Another method for treating tarnish involves applying a drop of water and a small amount of fluoride toothpaste onto a tissue. Gently rub the mixture onto the tarnished silver (or other metals, though silver is most commonly affected by tarnish) to restore its original luster.
